newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Zedillo welcomes Clinton as "good friend".
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Zedillo welcomes Clinton as "good friend".

text.p: President Bill Clinton called on Tuesday for Mexico and the United States to enter the next century together as "trusted friends" on the first full day of his state visit to the U.S.'s southern neighbour and third biggest trading partner.
"The success of Mexico's endeavours matters to the United States of America," Clinton said in a speech at the official welcoming ceremony in Mexico City.
"Our nations share far more than a common border. We share common challenges and common opportunities...we must meet the future together."
As cannons boomed out salutes under a blue sky and an honour guard stood to attention, Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo hailed Clinton as a "good friend of Mexico."

He recalled the U.S. leader's efforts to win congressional approval for the North American Free Trade Agreement and his pivotal role in the $13.5 billion American bailout of Mexico from financial crisis in 1995.
Ever mindful of strong Mexican nationalism, Zedillo was careful to point out that Clinton was "a friend who respects Mexico as a sovereign nation."
"We particularly value President Clinton's practice of dialogue and cooperation in dealing with the problems our two countries have in common," Zedillo said.
"Time and results have proved President Clinton right in his policy of respect and friendship toward Mexico."
Clinton stressed cooperation in his speech -- which he opened with the Spanish greeting "Saludos Amigos". He said the partnership between Mexico and the United States "has never been more important."
"In today's world, cooperation is the surest path to security, prosperity and peace," he added.
Trade between Mexico and the United States reached a record $140 billion last year and continues to grow.

Clinton also had warm words for Zedillo. He praised the Mexican leader's "bold leadership," economic reforms and encouragement of greater democracy. Mexico has been ruled by a single party since 1929.
After the speeches, the two leaders walked past a crowd of cheering schoolchildren waving Mexican and U.S. flags, Clinton using the help of crutches.
The two leaders then entered a private meeting where delicate topics such as drugs and migration will be discussed, officials said.
Neither president would answer a question on whether Zedillo had agreed to a U.S. request to allow American anti-drug agents here to carry weapons.
The warmth of the official welcome contrasted with the exceptionally tight security surrounding the visit and a more subdued mood among the Mexican people toward Clinton.
Many Mexicans have been angered by recent U.S. moves against illegal immigrants and what they see as preaching by Washington on how to fight the drug war.

A poll published on Tuesday by Reforma newspaper found that only 36 percent of Mexicans had a favourable opinion of the United States now, down from 62 percent a year ago -- before the recent disputes over drugs and migration.

Scattered protests greeted Clinton's arrival in Mexico on Monday, with left-wingers waving "Clinton Go Home" banners and a small group of demonstrators burning U.S. flags outside the American embassy.
Citizens grumbled about the hundreds of heavily armed troops and police blocking streets around the area of Clinton's hotel, causing traffic jams and delays.
"Why are there so many people armed?" a boy in a newspaper cartoon asked on Tuesday. "Because Clinton came on a friendly visit," snarled his mother in reply.
Most cruel of all was a cartoon in Reforma showing Clinton on crutches addressing a Zedillo with no legs perched on a trolley, his arm outstretched to the U.S. leader, apparently begging for help.
